prize_parts.citation: for an oeuvre that renews lyric, verse narrative and essay through hybrid forms, in a sustained dialogue with antiquity, grief and the fragment

statement.case_for: My configuration is unchanged: one prize part, Anne Carson. The exchange sharpened the reasons rather than replacing them. The case rests on an unmistakable voice and on formal invention that carries intellectual and emotional weight. Autobiography of Red recasts the Geryon myth as a verse novel. Nox turns elegy, philological commentary and fragmentary material into one work. The recurring concerns (the broken or lost text, grief, desire, the limits of translation) give the oeuvre a method that returns and develops across books rather than a series of one-off experiments. Round 1 showed that the main objections to this case concern citation scope, not the quality of the central books. I think that scope problem can be solved by drafting. The citation should name her own lyric, verse narrative and essay, with antiquity as the field of dialogue. Translation, scholarship and book design should be context, not credited achievements. That wording avoids a prize that reads as recognition of classical scholarship or of translation as such. It also answers the chair's point that the book design is part of how the text is composed and should not become a separate criterion. Much of her work is in English and often short, so it can be assessed with less translation loss than several other shortlisted writers. That is a practical advantage for our assessment and does not itself show greater merit. This is a judgment from public knowledge and the committee files, not a verified reading of the full corpus.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is still maturity. Much of the weight falls on a few celebrated books. Colleagues across both camps, and the chair summary, record that confidence in her later and more occasional output is lower, and I share that. Part of what is published later appears in performance or limited-edition formats, so the printed record may be thinner for the recent period. The hybrid and allusive forms are also harder to weigh against a long, consolidated body of work. Cărtărescu offers exactly that kind of long-form oeuvre, and his case is a serious competing claim. If members who know her wider output cannot show that the lesser-known books develop her concerns rather than vary the format, my preference should weaken. I would then move to B034, provided the question of excess in the late novels is answered better than it has been so far.

responses.point: Olsson says the citation should rest on Carson's renewal of lyric, essay and verse narrative, with antiquity as the field of dialogue and not as a credited scholarly achievement. He also says the printed record for the recent period may be thinner than for the major books.
responses.response: I agree, and I would hold to that wording in the private vote. His observation about the thinner printed record matters most for how the committee states its confidence. It should say plainly that the case is strongest for the central books and less certain for the later output. I do not want our shared first choice treated as evidence in itself. If the committee's reading of the later books shows variation of format without development, his criterion that a few works of lasting formal importance within a consistent method can suffice would carry more weight than mine. I would then have to ask whether a consistent method is actually shown.

responses.point: Sem-Sandberg proposes testing Cărtărescu by comparing the Orbitor trilogy with Solenoid for real development, and not relying on scale. He also asks whether Carson's depth holds beyond Autobiography of Red and Nox.
responses.response: His test is the right one for both candidates, and I would apply the same standard to Carson: the later books must show development of her concerns, not just new formats. One correction on my own position. In round 1 I listed the late-phase question as open for Cărtărescu. I did not claim to know that the late books deepen the project, and I cannot confirm it from translations. I accept his point that the burden falls on those who know the wider output to test the claim. I still think the translations and adaptations belong to the same project of treating the classical text as a fragment to be reworked. That is why I propose naming the scope in the citation without crediting translation as a separate achievement.

responses.point: Mattson treats Cărtărescu's density as part of the achievement and not a risk to it, and says this holds provided the late books show development. She also says her view is conditional on reading everything by the shortlisted writers.
responses.response: I accept the distinction, and it narrows our disagreement. Density can be part of the achievement, but that depends on its producing structure and sentence-level invention, which I cannot verify in Romanian. The same condition applies to my candidate, because formal inventiveness is only an achievement if it generates meaning. Her argument that a continuous long-form project makes the whole-oeuvre claim easier to assess is fair, and I take it seriously. I do not agree that this settles the comparison. Ease of assessment is a practical matter and does not show greater literary significance. I would not move to B034 on that argument alone.

responses.point: Carlberg ranks Carson second and says her difficulty is how to weigh the hybrid forms, the translated and scholarly material and the classical allusiveness. She says that if the citation rests on Carson's own lyric-essayistic work she would find her very close to Cărtărescu.
responses.response: That conditional is what I most wanted from this exchange. It shows that the citation scope, and not the quality of the books, is the real obstacle for the members who ranked her second. I think the narrow wording does meet her condition. The allusiveness question remains open, and I can only say that her central books work through emotional and formal movement without requiring the reader to hold the source texts in mind. She says Robinson's fiction is small and narrow in range. That is why I keep Robinson only as a distant alternative. I do not doubt the sentence-level achievement, but I would not set a smaller and narrower body of work above either of the two leading cases.

uncertainties: Whether Carson's later and more occasional work (including performance and limited-edition formats) matches the central books. My knowledge of the full corpus is partial and rests on public knowledge, not independent verification.
How far the book-object elements can be judged as literature on the page, and whether the narrow citation wording fully separates her own work from translation and scholarship.
Whether her allusive, classically informed English travels across languages and readers, a question I cannot settle for translations.

Whether Cărtărescu's very long novels sustain quality or become excessive, and how much of the Romanian prose density survives translation. I cannot verify the claim that his late phase deepens the project, and if it holds he may be the stronger oeuvre-wide candidate.
I cannot add direct knowledge of Michon's French or Adonis's Arabic, so my low rankings of both are provisional.
Carlberg's committee voting status is undocumented, so any count that includes her simulated vote is a modeling assumption.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile. My own fiction draws on myth, fairy tale and ekphrasis, and I wrote the Lagerlöf biography. I treat both as context only. They are not evidence that I favour any candidate, and no personal or institutional tie to any shortlisted writer is documented. My 2024 Nobel Museum interview was given on behalf of the committee and does not establish a personal preference. Conflicts are disclosed here and not adjudicated.
